claim: The salivary gland placode consists of about 100 epithelial cells.
source: Each of the two placodes on the ventral side of the embryo (Figure 1A) consists of about 100 epithelial cells, and cells in the dorso-posterior corner of the placode begin the process of tube formation through constriction of their apical surfaces, leading to the formation of an invagination pit through which all cells eventually internalise (Girdler and Röper, 2014; Sidor and Röper, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of cells in the placode and cites supporting references.

claim: Cells in the dorso-posterior corner of the placode begin tube formation through constriction of their apical surfaces.
source: Each of the two placodes on the ventral side of the embryo (Figure 1A) consists of about 100 epithelial cells, and cells in the dorso-posterior corner of the placode begin the process of tube formation through constriction of their apical surfaces, leading to the formation of an invagination pit through which all cells eventually internalise (Girdler and Röper, 2014; Sidor and Röper, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this process and cites supporting references.

claim: Apical constriction leads to the formation of an invagination pit through which all cells eventually internalize.
source: Each of the two placodes on the ventral side of the embryo (Figure 1A) consists of about 100 epithelial cells, and cells in the dorso-posterior corner of the placode begin the process of tube formation through constriction of their apical surfaces, leading to the formation of an invagination pit through which all cells eventually internalise (Girdler and Röper, 2014; Sidor and Röper, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this morphogenetic outcome and cites supporting references.

claim: Apical constriction is a cell behavior that can transform columnar or cuboidal cells into wedge-shaped cells.
source: Apical constriction, a cell behaviour of epithelial cells that can transform columnar or cuboidal cells into wedge-shaped cells and can thereby induce and assist tissue bending, has emerged as a key morphogenetic module utilised in many different events ranging from mesoderm invagination in flies, Xenopus and zebrafish to lens formation in the mouse eye (Lee and Harland, 2007; Martin and Goldstein, 2014; Martin et al., 2009; Plageman et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this cell behavior and cites multiple supporting references.

claim: Apical constriction can induce and assist tissue bending.
source: Apical constriction, a cell behaviour of epithelial cells that can transform columnar or cuboidal cells into wedge-shaped cells and can thereby induce and assist tissue bending, has emerged as a key morphogenetic module utilised in many different events ranging from mesoderm invagination in flies, Xenopus and zebrafish to lens formation in the mouse eye (Lee and Harland, 2007; Martin and Goldstein, 2014; Martin et al., 2009; Plageman et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this function and cites supporting references.

claim: Apical constriction relies on the apical accumulation of actomyosin.
source: Apical constriction relies on the apical accumulation of actomyosin, that when tied to junctional complexes can exert pulling forces on the cell cortex and thereby reduce apical cell radius (Blanchard et al., 2010; Mason et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the molecular mechanism and cites supporting references.

claim: Two pools of apical actomyosin have been identified: junctional actomyosin and apical-medial actomyosin.
source: Two pools of apical actomyosin have been identified: junctional actomyosin, closely associated with apical adherens junctions, as well as apical-medial actomyosin, a highly dynamic pool underlying the free apical domain (Levayer and Lecuit, 2012; Röper, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly identifies these two pools and cites supporting references.

claim: Cell intercalation is the directed exchange of neighbours that drives events such as convergence and extension of tissues during gastrulation.
source: Another prominent cell behaviour during morphogenesis in all animals is cell intercalation, the directed exchange of neighbours, that is for instance the driving force behind events such as convergence and extension of tissues during gastrulation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this cell behavior and its role.

claim: Apical actomyosin activity is crucial to junction shrinkage and junction extension during cell intercalation.
source: Also during cell intercalation apical actomyosin activity is crucial to processes such as junction shrinkage and junction extension that underlie this cell behaviour (Bertet et al., 2004; Collinet et al., 2015; Rauzi et al., 2010; Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this mechanism and cites supporting references.

claim: Force generated in one tissue can have profound effects on morphogenetic behaviour and cytoskeletal organisation in another tissue.
source: There is mounting evidence from different processes in Drosophila that force generated in one tissue can have profound effects on morphogenetic behaviour and cytoskeletal organisation in another tissue.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this principle based on evidence from Drosophila.

claim: During germband extension in the fly embryo, the pulling force exerted by the invagination of the posterior midgut leads to anisotropic cell shape changes in the germband cells.
source: For instance, during germband extension in the fly embryo, the pulling force exerted by the invagination of the posterior midgut leads to both anisotropic cell shape changes in the germband cells (Lye et al., 2015) and also assists the junction extension during neighbour exchanges (Collinet et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this example and cites supporting references.

claim: The pulling force from the posterior midgut assists junction extension during neighbour exchanges in the germband.
source: For instance, during germband extension in the fly embryo, the pulling force exerted by the invagination of the posterior midgut leads to both anisotropic cell shape changes in the germband cells (Lye et al., 2015) and also assists the junction extension during neighbour exchanges (Collinet et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this mechanism and cites supporting references.

claim: During mesoderm invagination in the fly embryo, anisotropic tension due to the elongated geometry of the embryo leads to anisotropic polarisation and activity of apical actomyosin within the mesodermal cells.
source: During mesoderm invagination in the fly embryo, anisotropic tension due to the elongated geometry of the embryo leads to a clear anisotropic polarisation and activity of apical actomyosin within the mesodermal cells (Chanet et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this mechanism and cites a supporting reference.

claim: Placodal cells contain prominent junctional and apical-medial actomyosin networks during early tube formation.
source: We have previously shown that in the salivary gland placode during early tube formation when the cells just start to invaginate, the placodal cells contain prominent junctional and apical-medial actomyosin networks (Booth et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation and cites a supporting reference.

claim: The highly dynamic and pulsatile apical-medial pool is important for apical constriction of the placodal cells.
source: The highly dynamic and pulsatile apical-medial pool is important for apical constriction of the placodal cells, and constriction starts in the position of the future pit and cells near the pit continue to constrict before they invaginate (Booth et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this function and cites a supporting reference.

claim: Constriction starts in the position of the future pit and cells near the pit continue to constrict before they invaginate.
source: The highly dynamic and pulsatile apical-medial pool is important for apical constriction of the placodal cells, and constriction starts in the position of the future pit and cells near the pit continue to constrict before they invaginate (Booth et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this spatial and temporal pattern and cites a supporting reference.

claim: Fog expression is upregulated in the salivary gland placode downstream of Fkh and Hkb.
source: The GPCR-ligand Fog is important for apical constriction and myosin activation in different contexts in the fly (Kerridge et al., 2016; Manning et al., 2013), and fog expression is also clearly upregulated in the salivary gland placode downstream of two transcription factors, Fkh and Hkb (Chung et al., 2017; Myat and Andrew, 2000b).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this regulatory relationship and cites supporting references.

claim: Fkh is a key factor expressed in the placode directly downstream of the homeotic factor Sex combs reduced (Scr).
source: Fkh is a key factor expressed in the placode directly downstream of the homeotic factor Sex combs reduced (Scr) that itself is necessary and sufficient to induce gland fate (Myat and Andrew, 2000a; Panzer et al., 1992).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this regulatory relationship and cites supporting references.

claim: Scr is necessary and sufficient to induce gland fate.
source: Fkh is a key factor expressed in the placode directly downstream of the homeotic factor Sex combs reduced (Scr) that itself is necessary and sufficient to induce gland fate (Myat and Andrew, 2000a; Panzer et al., 1992).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this function and cites supporting references.

claim: fkh mutants fail to invaginate cells from the placode, with only a central depression within the placode forming over time.
source: fkh mutants fail to invaginate cells from the placode, with only a central depression within the placode forming over time (Myat and Andrew, 2000a).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this mutant phenotype and cites a supporting reference.

claim: In addition to apical constriction, circumferentially oriented directional intercalation of placodal cells plays a major contribution to ordered invagination at early stages.
source: In addition to previously characterised apical constriction (Booth et al., 2014; Chung et al., 2017), we demonstrate that circumferentially oriented directional intercalation of placodal cells plays a major contribution to ordered invagination at early stages.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding as a key result of the study.

claim: Near the pit of invagination, isotropic apical constriction leads to strong cell-wedging.
source: Extending analyses in 3D, we find that near the pit of invagination, isotropic apical constriction leads to strong cell-wedging.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding from 3D analysis.

claim: Further from the pit cells interleave circumferentially, suggesting apically driven behaviours.
source: Further from the pit cells interleave circumferentially, suggesting apically driven behaviours.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation and its interpretation.

claim: Junctional myosin is enriched in the circumferential orientation.
source: Supporting this, junctional myosin is enriched in, and neighbour exchanges are biased towards the circumferential orientation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation as supporting evidence.

claim: Neighbour exchanges are biased towards the circumferential orientation.
source: Supporting this, junctional myosin is enriched in, and neighbour exchanges are biased towards the circumferential orientation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation as supporting evidence.

claim: In a mutant failing pit specification, neither myosin enrichment nor neighbour exchanges are biased due to an inactive pit.
source: In a mutant failing pit specification, neither are biased due to an inactive pit.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding from mutant analysis.

claim: Tube budding involves radially patterned pools of apical myosin, medial as well as junctional.
source: Thus, tube budding involves radially patterned pools of apical myosin, medial as well as junctional, and radially patterned 3D-cell behaviours, with a close mechanical interplay between invagination and intercalation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion from the study.

claim: Tube budding involves radially patterned 3D-cell behaviours.
source: Thus, tube budding involves radially patterned pools of apical myosin, medial as well as junctional, and radially patterned 3D-cell behaviours, with a close mechanical interplay between invagination and intercalation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion from the study.

claim: There is a close mechanical interplay between invagination and intercalation during tube budding.
source: Thus, tube budding involves radially patterned pools of apical myosin, medial as well as junctional, and radially patterned 3D-cell behaviours, with a close mechanical interplay between invagination and intercalation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion from the study.

claim: Apical constriction at the invagination point preceded actual tissue bending.
source: Apical constriction at this point in fact preceded actual tissue bending (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this temporal relationship and references Figure 1B showing the observation.

claim: Apical constriction is clustered around the pit and is important for proper tissue invagination and tube formation.
source: We have previously shown that apical constriction is clustered around the pit and is important for proper tissue invagination and tube formation (Booth et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this previous finding and cites a supporting reference.

claim: The invagination pit is located at the dorsal-posterior edge rather than within the centre of the placode.
source: Within this circular patch, the invagination pit is located at the dorsal-posterior edge rather than within the centre of the placode.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this spatial organization.

claim: Dynamic analysis revealed distinct zones of apical cell behaviour in the placode.
source: Dynamic analysis of the changes in apical area of placodal cells, in the time interval of 18 min prior to and 18 min after the first tissue bending, revealed distinct zones of apical cell behaviour.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding from dynamic analysis.

claim: There is a clear split into cells whose apical area did not change or changed only slightly and cells whose apical area progressively decreased.
source: Grouping the placodal cells into ~ 2 cell-wide stripes concentric to the pit for apical area change analysis (Figure 1G; Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Video 2) revealed a split into cells whose apical area over this time interval did not change or changed only slightly (Figure 1G', red, yellow and green lines) and cells whose apical area progressively decreased (Figure 1G', blue and purple lines).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Cell divisions have ceased in the placode around the time of specification.
source: Cell divisions have ceased in the placode around the time of specification, and there is also no cell death, therefore none of these processes contributed to the overall tissue deformation in this case.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: There is no cell death in the placode during the analyzed period.
source: Cell divisions have ceased in the placode around the time of specification, and there is also no cell death, therefore none of these processes contributed to the overall tissue deformation in this case.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Strong isotropic tissue contraction near the invagination pit was mainly contributed by apical cell constriction.
source: Spatial plots summarising ~ 36 mins of data centred around the first tissue bending event (combined from the analysis of 9 wild-type embryos; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) revealed strong isotropic tissue contraction near the invagination pit (Figure 2C' and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, green) that was mainly contributed by apical cell constriction (Figure 2C'' and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: At a distance from the pit, tissue elongation dominated in the radial direction and was contributed mostly by cell intercalation.
source: At a distance from the pit, tissue elongation dominated in the radial direction (Figure 2C', magenta) and was contributed mostly by cell intercalation (Figure 2C'',C''').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Apical cell constriction began more than 10 min before any curvature change at the tissue level.
source: At the whole tissue level, apical cell constriction began more than 10 min before any curvature change at the tissue level (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,C', green curve), and this change was most pronounced in the cells near the invagination pit (Figure 2D,D' versus E, E', green curve).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this temporal relationship and references figures showing the data.

claim: Cell intercalation commenced about 10 min prior to tissue bending.
source: In addition, cell intercalation also commenced about 10 min prior to tissue bending (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,C', orange curve), but in this case, the stronger contribution came from cells far from the pit (Figure 2E,E' versus D,D', orange curve).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this temporal relationship and references figures showing the data.

claim: Constriction was isotropic near the pit, with equally large magnitudes contributing both radially and circumferentially.
source: Although constriction was isotropic near the pit, with equally large magnitudes contributing both radially and circumferentially (Figure 2D,D', green curves), intercalation was clearly polarised towards the invagination pit, with expansion radially in the orientation of the pit (Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, 'rad', orange curves), and contraction circumferentially (Figure 2D',E' and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C', 'circ', orange curves; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Intercalation was clearly polarised towards the invagination pit, with expansion radially and contraction circumferentially.
source: Although constriction was isotropic near the pit, with equally large magnitudes contributing both radially and circumferentially (Figure 2D,D', green curves), intercalation was clearly polarised towards the invagination pit, with expansion radially in the orientation of the pit (Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, 'rad', orange curves), and contraction circumferentially (Figure 2D',E' and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C', 'circ', orange curves; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Directional cell intercalation constitutes a major second cell behaviour occurring during tissue bending and invagination of a tube.
source: Thus, in addition to apical constriction, directional cell intercalation constitutes a major second cell behaviour occurring during tissue bending and invagination of a tube.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The amount of both cell behaviours occurring was radially patterned across the placode.
source: Furthermore, the amount of both cell behaviours occurring was radially patterned across the placode.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this spatial pattern.

claim: Placodal cells extend up to 15 µm in depth.
source: For instance, in the case of the salivary gland placode, cells extend up to 15 µm in depth (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this measurement and references a figure showing the data.

claim: The spatial pattern of change at mid-basal level was similar to changes within the apical domain.
source: Overall, the spatial pattern of change at mid-basal level was similar to changes within the apical domain during 33 min centred around the start of tissue bending (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this comparison and references figures showing the data.

claim: Isotropic tissue contraction at mid-basal depth was clustered around the position of the invagination pit and was due to cell constriction at this level.
source: Isotropic tissue contraction at mid-basal depth was clustered around the position of the invagination pit (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C, green), and this was due to cell constriction at this level (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B',C'), whereas the tissue expansion at a distance from the pit in the radial direction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) was due primarily to cell intercalation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C'').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Tissue expansion at a distance from the pit in the radial direction was due primarily to cell intercalation.
source: Isotropic tissue contraction at mid-basal depth was clustered around the position of the invagination pit (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C, green), and this was due to cell constriction at this level (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B',C'), whereas the tissue expansion at a distance from the pit in the radial direction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) was due primarily to cell intercalation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C'').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Isotropic cell constriction dominated apically in cells near the pit, but with a slower rate of constriction at the mid-basal depth.
source: In temporally resolved plots, isotropic cell constriction dominated apically in cells near the pit (Figure 3D, pink), but with a slower rate of constriction at the mid-basal depth (Figure 3D, blue).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Near the pit and once tissue-bending had commenced, the basal surface of the cells was displaced even further basally than in the rest of the placode, and cells were expanded at this level, leading to an overall wedge-shape.
source: This was confirmed by cross-section images that show that, near the pit and once tissue-bending had commenced, the basal surface of the cells was displaced even further basally than in the rest of the placode, and cells were expanded at this level, leading to an overall wedge-shape (Figure 1B').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation and references a figure showing the data.

claim: Intercalation behaviour appeared to be highly coordinated between apical and basal levels with near identical contributions at both particularly in cells far from the pit.
source: In contrast to cell shape changes that diverged at depth at least in the cells near the pit, intercalation behaviour appeared to be highly coordinated between apical and basal levels with near identical contributions at both particularly in cells far from the pit (Figure 3D', E' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D'').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Cells across the placode started out at −18 min before pit invagination unwedged and mostly untilted in radial and circumferential orientations.
source: Cells across the placode started out at −18 min before pit invagination unwedged and mostly untilted in radial and circumferential orientations (Figure 4B',D').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this initial condition and references figures showing the data.

claim: Cells near the pit became progressively wedge-shaped over the next 30 min, with smaller apices.
source: Cells near the pit became progressively wedge-shaped over the next 30 min, with smaller apices (Figure 4B', orange lines; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Cell wedging was reasonably isotropic, but with circumferential wedging always stronger than radial.
source: Cell wedging was reasonably isotropic, but with circumferential wedging always stronger than radial.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Away from the pit, progressive wedging was less rapid, again with a strong circumferential contribution but nearly no radial contribution.
source: Away from the pit, progressive wedging was less rapid, again with a strong circumferential contribution but nearly no radial contribution (Figure 4B', purple lines).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references a figure showing the data.

claim: Circumferential interleaving was always more negative than radial interleaving, often significantly so.
source: Indeed, circumferential interleaving was always more negative than radial interleaving, often significantly so (Figure 4C', solid vs dashed lines).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references a figure showing the data.

claim: Interleaving contributes a circumferential tissue contraction apically, with a concomitant radial expansion.
source: Thus, interleaving contributes a circumferential tissue contraction apically, with a concomitant radial expansion.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation of the interleaving pattern.

claim: Cell tilt increased continuously in the radial direction towards the pit over the period of analysis.
source: Cell tilt, a measure of the divergence of a cell's in-line from the surface normal (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B,D), increased continuously in the radial direction towards the pit over the period of our analysis (Figure 4D', solid lines).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: A stronger tilt was observed for the cells further from the pit.
source: A stronger tilt was observed for the cells further from the pit (Figure 4D', purple solid line), which is expected from the radial wedging seen near the pit (Figure 4B', solid orange line).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: The relatively isotropic rates of apical constriction near the pit and the very similar rates of intercalation apically versus basally were in fact grounded in anisotropic wedging near the pit and in an interleaving difference between apical and basal.
source: Hence, the relatively isotropic rates of apical constriction near the pit and the very similar rates of intercalation apically versus basally were in fact grounded in anisotropic wedging near the pit and in an interleaving difference between apical and basal.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation connecting 2D and 3D observations.

claim: 3D tissue information such as wedging, interleaving and tilt are essential to fully understand planar cell behaviours such as cell shape change and intercalation.
source: 3D tissue information such as wedging, interleaving and tilt are therefore essential to fully understand planar cell behaviours such as cell shape change and intercalation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion from the 3D analysis.

claim: T1 exchanges occurred at a constant rate over the study period.
source: T1s occurred at a constant rate over our study period, and we observed T1s in both orientations, revealing that neighbour connectivity was quite dynamic (Figure 5C',D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Over two-thirds of neighbour gains were oriented circumferentially.
source: Nevertheless, over two-thirds of neighbour gains were oriented circumferentially, a bias that correlates with the intercalation strain rate contraction circumferentially (see for example Figure 2E').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references a figure showing the data.

claim: The proportion of productive circumferential gains was approximately constant.
source: The proportion of productive circumferential gains was approximately constant, which lead to a steady net gain over time (Figure 5C'').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references a figure showing the data.

claim: The cumulative strain attributable to discrete T1s is in good agreement with the cumulative strain attributed to the continuous process of intercalation.
source: Furthermore, the cumulative strain attributable to discrete T1s calculated here (e0.09 = 1.09) is in good agreement with the cumulative strain over the same time window that is attributed to the continuous process of intercalation (1.1 in Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this comparison and references a figure.

claim: Rosette formation began prior to the first sign of tissue-bending, but the number of rosettes per placode increased afterwards.
source: Rosette formation began prior to the first sign of tissue-bending, but the number of rosettes per placode increased afterwards (Figure 5E,E').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this temporal pattern and references figures showing the data.

claim: Rosettes were usually formed of five to seven cells, with most involving only five cells.
source: Rosettes were usually formed of five to seven cells, with most involving only five cells (Figure 5E', F).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Groups of cells contracted in a circumferential orientation to form a rosette, the resolution of which then moved individual cells towards the invaginating pit.
source: Analysis of rosette formation and resolution in our time-lapse datasets of embryos expressing a membrane marker demonstrated that groups of cells contracted in a circumferential orientation to form a rosette, the resolution of which then moved individual cells towards the invaginating pit (Figure 5F and Video 5), thereby leading to the expansion observed in the strain rate analysis.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this observation and references a figure and video showing the data.

claim: In all individual rosette formation-resolution examples analysed, junctional myosin II appeared particularly enriched in the form of short cable-like structures at the central contact sites of the rosette.
source: In all individual rosette formation-resolution examples analysed (n = 29), junctional myosin II appeared particularly enriched in the form of short cable-like structures at the central contact sites of the rosette (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation and references figures showing the data.

claim: Myosin cables initially spanned several cell diameters and shortened concomitant with the cells being drawn into a central vertex.
source: These cables initially spanned several cell diameters and shortened concomitant with the cells being drawn into a central vertex (Figure 5I).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this dynamic behavior and references a figure showing the data.

claim: Junction lengths were shorter than Voronoi predicted lengths for shortening T1 junctions compared to non-T1 junctions, most strongly for circumferentially oriented junctions.
source: In the salivary gland placode, junction lengths were shorter than Voronoi predicted lengths for shortening T1 junctions compared to non-T1 junctions, most strongly for circumferentially oriented junctions (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Circumferential non-T1 interfaces deviated from neutral geometries by being shorter on average than expected, with radial junctions longer.
source: Circumferential non-T1 interfaces also deviated from neutral geometries by being shorter on average than expected, with radial junctions longer (Figure 6F).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references a figure showing the data.

claim: Angles linked to circumferential junctions were more acute, relative to neutral Voronoi geometry, than those linked to radial junctions.
source: On average, angles linked to circumferential junctions were indeed more acute, relative to neutral Voronoi geometry, than those linked to radial junctions (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Cells were on average more elongated circumferentially.
source: Similarly, cells were on average more elongated circumferentially (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) as predicted by actively contracting circumferential junctions and incompatible with a radial pull.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: These three geometrical measures for cells far from the pit are consistent with an active intercalation mechanism, leading to circumferential neighbour gains and thus circumferential convergence.
source: These three geometrical measures for cells far from the pit, where intercalation dominates, are therefore consistent with an active intercalation mechanism, leading to circumferential neighbour gains and thus circumferential convergence.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation of the geometrical measures.

claim: A clear enrichment of myosin II was apparent in circumferentially compared to radially oriented junctions.
source: When apical junctional myosin intensity was quantified in fixed samples of sqhGFP embryos across the early placode, a clear enrichment of myosin II was apparent in circumferentially compared to radially oriented junctions (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Tissue-wide circumferential versus radial polarisation of myosin clearly supported an active mechanism of cell intercalation.
source: Such tissue-wide circumferential versus radial polarisation of myosin clearly supported an active mechanism of cell intercalation, with circumferential myosin II likely assisting both rosette and T1 vertex formation during the polarised cell intercalation events.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation of the myosin polarization data.

claim: Starting about 10 min prior to tissue bending, bi-polar enrichment of myosin II at circumferential junctions was significantly stronger than at radial junctions when measured across the whole placode.
source: Starting about 10 min prior to tissue bending, bi-polar enrichment of myosin II at circumferential junctions was significantly stronger than at radial junctions when measured across the whole placode (Figure 7E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references a figure showing the data.

claim: Starting ~ 5 min later, unipolar enrichment of myosin II at circumferential junctions dominated over radial enrichment when measured across the whole placode.
source: Similarly, starting ~ 5 min later, unipolar enrichment of myosin II at circumferential junctions dominated over radial enrichment when measured across the whole placode (Figure 7F).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references a figure showing the data.

claim: This clear and increasing circumferential junctional polarisation of myosin II together with the geometrical signatures strongly supported an active mechanism of T1 vertex and rosette formation.
source: This clear and increasing circumferential junctional polarisation of myosin II together with the geometrical signatures discussed above strongly supported an active mechanism of T1 vertex and rosette formation (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation and references a figure.

claim: Antibody labelling of Baz often showed a complementarity in membrane enrichment to myosin II.
source: Antibody labelling of Baz often showed a complementarity in membrane enrichment to myosin II (Figure 7G–I), most pronounced where myosin II was organised into circumferential mini cables during intercalation events (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation and references figures showing the data.

claim: Baz was enriched at radially oriented junctions where myosin II was low, and vice versa at circumferential junctions.
source: Baz was enriched at radially oriented junctions where myosin II was low, and vice versa at circumferential junctions, though in contrast to germband extension, the Baz polarisation did not extend uniformly across the tissue and was overall less strong than the myosin II polarisation (Figure 7I).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references a figure showing the data.

claim: A conserved molecular pattern of myosin-Baz complementarity is imprinted onto the salivary gland placode in a radial coordinate pattern.
source: Thus, in order to adapt to a circular tissue geometry and to the need for ordered invagination through a focal point during the process of tube budding, a conserved molecular pattern of myosin-Baz complementarity is apparently imprinted onto the salivary gland placode in a radial coordinate pattern, rather than the prevailing A-P/D-V pattern of the earlier embryo during germband extension (Figure 7J,K).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation and references figures showing the comparison.

claim: Fkh is expressed just upon specification of the placodal cells in a dynamic pattern spreading across the whole placode.
source: Fkh is expressed just upon specification of the placodal cells in a dynamic pattern spreading across the whole placode (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–C), directly downstream of the homeotic factor Scr (Zhou et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this expression pattern and references figures and a citation.

claim: In fkh mutants, invagination of the placode fails, and towards the end of embryogenesis salivary gland-fated cells undergo apoptosis.
source: In fkh mutants, invagination of the placode fails, and towards the end of embryogenesis salivary gland-fated cells undergo apoptosis as Fkh appears to prevent activation of pro-apoptotic factors (Jürgens and Weigel, 1988; Myat and Andrew, 2000a).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this mutant phenotype and cites supporting references.

claim: fkh mutant placodes showed no sign of a dorsal-posterior invagination point at late stage 11.
source: When fkh mutant placodes were compared to wild-type ones at late stage 11 (beyond the time window analysed here) then fkh mutant placodes showed no sign of a dorsal-posterior invagination point (Figure 8A–B'; Figure 8—figure supplement 1D–E'').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation and references figures showing the data.

claim: Many fkh mutant placodes beyond late stage 11 showed a centrally located shallow depression.
source: In fact, many placodes beyond late stage 11 showed a centrally located shallow depression (Figure 8A,A', yellow dotted lines).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation and references a figure showing the data.

claim: Strain rate analysis of fkh[6] mutant placodes showed that there was no constriction at the tissue level near the pit.
source: Strain rate analysis of five segmented movies of fkh[6] mutant placodes, spanning the equivalent time period to the wild-type movies analysed above (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C), showed that there was no constriction at the tissue level near the pit (Figure 8C–E and Figure 8—figure supplement 2D,D').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: In fkh[6] mutant placodes, there was a slight tissue expansion caused by a slight expansion at the cell level, with zero intercalation.
source: In fact, if anything, there was a slight tissue expansion (Figure 8E) caused by a slight expansion at the cell level (Figure 8E'), with zero intercalation (Figure 8E'').
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: At the tissue-level there was a strong and significant reduction in myosin II polarisation in fkh[6] mutants, with no difference between radial and circumferential orientations in either measure and myosin II bi-polarity indistinguishable from zero.
source: When myosin II unipolarity and bi-polarity were quantified from five segmented and tracked movies, at the tissue-level there was a strong and significant reduction in myosin II polarisation, with no difference between radial and circumferential orientations in either measure and myosin II bi-polarity indistinguishable from zero (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Neighbour exchanges were present in fkh[6] mutants, both in form of T1 exchanges and rosettes.
source: Nonetheless, cells were not static but in fact neighbour exchanges were present, both in form of T1 exchanges and rosettes (Figure 9C–F).

claim: In the fkh[6] mutant, circumferential and radial gains occurred in equal amounts leading to a near zero net gain.
source: However, in contrast to the control, where circumferential gains significantly outweighed radial neighbour gains leading to a positive net rate of productive circumferential gains (Figure 9F, green line), in the fkh[6] mutant circumferential and radial gains occurred in equal amounts (Figure 9E) leading to a near zero net gain (Figure 9F, pink line).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: Despite a loss of tissue-wide myosin II polarisation in fkh mutants, myosin II was still enriched at the central constricting junctions during individual rosette events.
source: Interestingly, when focusing on individual events such as rosettes, despite a loss of tissue-wide myosin II polarisation, myosin II was still enriched at the central constricting junctions (Figure 9Cd'), and in fixed embryos smaller regions of myosin II-Baz complementarity could be identified (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation and references figures showing the data.

claim: The ongoing but unproductive intercalations in the fkh mutant support the notion that the pulling of the constricting and invaginating pit reinforces the directionality of resolution in the wild type.
source: The ongoing but unproductive intercalations in the fkh mutant, that lack directional formation and resolution, support the notion that the pulling of the constricting and invaginating pit reinforces the directionality of resolution in the wild type.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation of the fkh mutant data.

claim: During tube formation of the salivary glands in the fly embryo, we observe a clear tissue-level radial organisation of cell behaviours, with the off-centre located invaginating pit as the organising focal point.
source: During tube formation of the salivary glands in the fly embryo, we observe a clear tissue-level radial organisation of cell behaviours, with the off-centre located invaginating pit as the organising focal point (Figure 10A).

claim: When analysed in 2D within the apical domain of the placodal epithelial cells, apical constriction dominates at the future pit of invagination and directional cell intercalation dominates further away from the pit.
source: When analysed in 2D within the apical domain of the placodal epithelial cells, apical constriction dominates at the future pit of invagination and directional cell intercalation dominates further away from the pit.

source: Our data at depth reveal that there is close coordination of intercalation rates between apical and mid-basal levels, and that the apically led interleaving and progressive wedging strongly support an active apical mechanism that is followed further basally.
